title: Physics 12 · Anchor Item Misconception Map
coveragePolicy: reviewed-anchor-items; reviewed distractor mappings are used when present; unmapped items fall back to the shared reasoning-category remediation layer

legacy-1.correctRationale: Displacement is a vector change in position and can be zero even after traveling a nonzero distance.

distractors.rationale: Distance is nonnegative path length; displacement magnitude can be smaller than distance.
Displacement is a length quantity and carries distance units such as meters.
Returning to the starting position gives zero displacement despite nonzero distance traveled.

legacy-2.correctRationale: The slope of a position-time graph is velocity.

distractors.rationale: Acceleration is the slope of a velocity-time graph, not a position-time graph.
Force is not obtained directly from the slope of position versus time.
Energy is not represented by the slope of a position-time graph.

legacy-3.correctRationale: Signed area under a velocity-time graph gives displacement.

distractors.rationale: Force is not the integral of velocity over time.
Power is energy transfer per time, not area under a velocity-time graph.
Pressure is force per area and is unrelated to integrating velocity over time.

legacy-4.correctRationale: Constant speed in a circle still means changing velocity direction, so acceleration is present.

distractors.rationale: Acceleration in circular motion does not require changing mass.
Acceleration can result from changing velocity direction even when speed stays constant.
Uniform circular motion requires inward net force to produce centripetal acceleration.

legacy-5.correctRationale: A scientific model states assumptions, generates testable predictions, and is checked against data.

distractors.rationale: Residuals are evidence about model adequacy and should be examined, not hidden.
Real data include uncertainty; exact fit is not required and can indicate overfitting.
Physical models require consistent quantities and units for meaningful comparison.

legacy-6.correctRationale: Newton's first law describes inertia and constant velocity when net external force is zero.

distractors.rationale: Newton's first law is about motion and net force, not creation of energy.
Electric charge is unrelated to the statement of Newton's first law.
Wave interference is not the subject of Newton's first law.

legacy-7.correctRationale: Newton's second law relates net force, mass, and acceleration.

distractors.rationale: Temperature and volume belong to thermodynamic relationships, not Newton's second law.
Charge and current describe electrical systems, not F=ma.
Wavelength and frequency are wave quantities, not the variables in Newton's second law.

legacy-8.correctRationale: Third-law forces are equal and opposite interaction forces acting on two different objects.

distractors.rationale: Forces on the same object are not a Newton's third-law pair.
Interaction forces exist whether objects are moving or not.
Newton's third law applies broadly to interactions, not only gravity.

legacy-9.correctRationale: Centripetal acceleration points toward the center of curvature.

distractors.rationale: Velocity is tangent to the path; centripetal acceleration is inward.
In an inertial-frame analysis, the acceleration is toward, not away from, the center.
Centripetal acceleration is generally perpendicular to instantaneous velocity, not opposite it.

legacy-10.correctRationale: An orbit can be modeled as continuous free fall with sufficient tangential velocity.

distractors.rationale: Orbiting objects remain under gravitational influence.
Changing velocity direction in orbit means nonzero centripetal acceleration.
Orbital motion is explained by Newtonian dynamics within its domain of validity.

legacy-11.correctRationale: Work depends on force, displacement, and the angle between them.

distractors.rationale: Mass alone does not determine work done by a force.
Time can matter for power, but work is not determined by time alone.
Temperature alone does not determine mechanical work.

legacy-12.correctRationale: Energy conservation requires a clearly defined system boundary and accounting for transfers across it.

distractors.rationale: Energy may leave a chosen system but is not assumed to vanish.
Friction can transform mechanical energy into thermal energy; conservation still applies to total energy with proper accounting.
Mass can be essential in gravitational or kinetic energy calculations.

legacy-13.correctRationale: Power is the rate of energy transfer or work.

distractors.rationale: Momentum is mass times velocity, not energy transfer per unit time.
Force per area defines pressure, not power.
Charge per time defines electric current, not power.

legacy-14.correctRationale: Efficiency compares useful output energy or power with total input.

distractors.rationale: Mass divided by volume defines density, not efficiency.
Force divided by acceleration relates to mass in Newtonian mechanics, not efficiency.
Wavelength/frequency ratios are not the definition of engineering efficiency.

legacy-15.correctRationale: Impulse equals change in momentum and also equals the time integral of force.

distractors.rationale: Impulse concerns change in momentum, not merely change in mass.
Kinetic energy and impulse are distinct quantities with different units and relationships.
Pressure-volume products are not the definition of impulse.

legacy-16.correctRationale: System momentum is conserved when net external impulse is negligible.

distractors.rationale: Momentum can be conserved in inelastic collisions where kinetic energy is not conserved.
Objects do not need to stop for system momentum to be conserved.
Internal forces can be large; their impulses exchange momentum within the system.

legacy-17.correctRationale: A perfectly inelastic collision is idealized by objects sticking together after impact.

distractors.rationale: Perfectly inelastic collisions conserve momentum for an isolated system but not kinetic energy.
The initial system momentum need not be zero.
Inelastic collisions commonly involve deformation or internal-energy increase.

legacy-18.correctRationale: For the same momentum change, increasing stopping time reduces average force.

distractors.rationale: For fixed impulse, average force is inversely related to stopping time.
Changing stopping time does not by itself determine whether total system momentum is conserved.
If momentum changes, impulse is nonzero even when the interaction lasts longer.

legacy-19.correctRationale: Torque magnitude depends on force and the perpendicular lever arm.

distractors.rationale: Mass can influence force, but torque is set by force and perpendicular distance from the axis.
Velocity is not part of the basic torque expression τ=r⊥F.
Temperature is not a defining variable in mechanical torque.

legacy-20.correctRationale: Angular momentum is conserved when net external torque is negligible.

distractors.rationale: Angular momentum conservation depends on external torque, not simply net force.
Rotating systems can conserve angular momentum while continuing to rotate.
Moment of inertia may change while angular speed changes so total angular momentum remains constant.

legacy-21.correctRationale: A rolling object can have both translational and rotational kinetic energy.

distractors.rationale: A moving rolling object generally has kinetic energy, not only potential energy.
Rolling includes rotation about the object's center of mass.
A translating rolling object has linear momentum.

legacy-22.correctRationale: Frequency is the reciprocal of period: f=1/T.

distractors.rationale: Amplitude measures maximum displacement, not cycle timing.
Mass can affect some oscillators, but frequency is not defined as 1/mass.
Frequency is a temporal rate, not the reciprocal of energy.

legacy-23.correctRationale: Wave speed equals frequency times wavelength: v=fλ.

distractors.rationale: Dimensional analysis shows f/λ does not have units of speed.
This expression has incorrect dimensions for speed.
v=ma mixes wave variables with Newton's second law and is not a wave-speed relation.

legacy-24.correctRationale: Resonance occurs when a driving frequency is near a system's natural frequency.

distractors.rationale: Resonance requires periodic driving, not removal of all frequencies.
Resonance is associated with enhanced amplitude under suitable conditions, not zero amplitude.
Resonance and interference are distinct wave phenomena; resonance does not imply waves cannot interfere.

legacy-25.correctRationale: Archimedes' principle relates buoyant force to the weight of displaced fluid.

distractors.rationale: Color does not determine displaced-fluid weight.
Electric charge is not the governing quantity in Archimedean buoyancy.
Sound frequency does not define buoyant force.

legacy-26.correctRationale: Conduction transfers thermal energy through microscopic interactions in contacting matter.

distractors.rationale: Bulk fluid motion is convection, not conduction.
Electromagnetic transfer is radiation, not conduction.
Nuclear decay is unrelated to the ordinary mechanism of thermal conduction.

legacy-27.correctRationale: Electric field is force per unit positive test charge.

distractors.rationale: Energy per mass is not electric field; electric potential is energy per charge.
Current and resistance are circuit quantities and do not define electric field.
Force per area defines pressure, not electric field.

legacy-28.correctRationale: For an ohmic element, Ohm's law relates voltage, current, and resistance.

distractors.rationale: Force, mass, and acceleration belong to Newton's second law.
Frequency and wavelength describe waves, not the V-I-R relation.
Pressure and volume belong to fluid/thermodynamic relationships, not Ohm's law.

legacy-29.correctRationale: Electromagnetic induction involves emf associated with changing magnetic flux.

distractors.rationale: Mass by itself does not generate induction current.
Sound does not directly create electric charge in the induction model.
A constant magnetic field does not by itself guarantee induced emf; changing flux is required.

legacy-30.correctRationale: Discrete digital states can be regenerated despite some noise, improving robust information transfer.

distractors.rationale: Digital information still requires physical storage or transmission media.
Digital encoding does not permit faster-than-light information transfer.
Digital information can be copied; discrete encoding can make copies highly reliable.

w6b.correctRationale: FBDs show forces on the selected object.

distractors.rationale: A free-body diagram includes forces acting on the chosen object, not forces it exerts elsewhere.
Velocity describes motion and is not drawn as a force vector.
A valid diagram includes all relevant forces on the object, not gravity alone.

distractors.rationale: Static friction can point inward when it provides the required centripetal force.

w13b.correctRationale: System boundaries make energy accounting meaningful.

distractors.rationale: Choosing a desired conclusion before defining the system biases the audit.
Energy audits should account for all relevant inputs/outputs and losses, not only one pathway.

w16a.correctRationale: Sticking together defines a perfectly inelastic collision.

distractors.rationale: Sticking together is the defining idealization of a perfectly inelastic collision, not elastic.
Static equilibrium describes zero net force/torque, not two objects sticking after impact.
Uniform circular motion is unrelated to collision classification.

w16b.correctRationale: Momentum is conserved but kinetic energy decreases.

distractors.rationale: In a perfectly inelastic collision, kinetic energy decreases even though momentum is conserved.
The sticking process does not increase kinetic energy in this isolated idealization.
The final kinetic energy is well-defined and calculable from the combined mass and final speed.

w19b.correctRationale: Angular rate is common; linear quantities depend on radius.

distractors.rationale: Linear speed increases with radius even when angular velocity is shared.

w25b.correctRationale: Opposite phase can reduce resultant amplitude.
